topic.angle: A burger as a currency yardstick

body.claim: The Economist has published the Big Mac Index since 1986, an informal way of measuring the purchasing power parity between two currencies.
body.why: The index was introduced in September 1986 by Pam Woodall as a semi-humorous illustration of PPP. The Economist proposed that a single McDonald's Big Mac could be used instead of a basket of goods, because of the prevalence of the fast food chain worldwide.

probes.question: Which publication introduced the Big Mac Index?
True or false: the Big Mac Index gave rise to the word "burgernomics".

image_brief.show: A hamburger on a plain background

claims.claim: The Economist has published the Big Mac Index since 1986, an informal way of measuring PPP between two currencies (claim; probe p1 answer The Economist)
claims.quote: a price index published since 1986 by The Economist as an informal way of measuring the purchasing power parity (PPP) between two currencies

claims.claim: Introduced in September 1986 by Pam Woodall as a semi-humorous illustration of PPP (why)
claims.quote: introduced in The Economist in September 1986 by Pam Woodall as a semi-humorous illustration of PPP

claims.claim: The Economist proposed a single Big Mac instead of a basket of goods (why)
claims.quote: The Economist proposed that a single McDonald's Big Mac could be used instead of a basket of goods.

claims.claim: Big Mac chosen because of the chain's worldwide prevalence (why)
claims.quote: A McDonald's Big Mac was chosen because of the prevalence of the fast food chain worldwide

claims.claim: The index gave rise to the word burgernomics (probe p2 true)
claims.quote: The index also gave rise to the word burgernomics.
